title: Mini-burst latency spectrogram — cribsheet
content:
Purpose: quick reference for thinking about tiny, frequent spikes (mini-bursts) and how different decode modes, batching windows, and quant profiles shape the instantaneous latency distribution and marginal token cost. This is intentionally terse — meant for on-call, design huddles, and spec appendices.

Executive summary:
- Mini-bursts (~5–40 concurrent short requests lasting 100–600ms) create a distinct latency footprint vs sustained throughput.
- Short-window batching (6–25ms gather) reduces per-token cost but introduces p99 tail mass from queuing; preemptive multiplex (slotization) reduces tail but increases amortized cost.
- Lightweight KV-prefetch (session-key hinting) recovers ~15–30% of observed p99 in our samples when hit rates > 0.6.

Test bed and knobs:
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB equivalent (prod-like), isolated instance, single infer worker.
- Models: rw-open-7b (float16), rw-open-13b (8-bit quantized), rw-compact-3b (FP16 low-latency profile).
- Workload: synthetic mini-burst generator (see linked artifacts), Poisson base rate 2 rps, burst events inject 5–40 concurrent 1–3 turn short sessions.
- Modes compared: immediate-forward (no batching), short-window batch (12ms gather), opportunistic multiplex (slot size 8 slots/slot-time 20ms), predictive-prefetch (session hints), kv-caching on/off, decode-mode sync vs async.

Key metrics collected (for each experiment): p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), mean tokens/sec, tokens-per-dollar (token cost normalized), per-request CPU/GPU time, queueing delay fraction.

Representative measured slice (rw-open-7b, median of 40 runs per config):

Config | p50 | p90 | p99 | tokens/sec | token-$ (normalized)
-----------------------------------------------------------
immediate-forward | 32ms | 78ms | 220ms | 240 | 1.00
12ms-batch | 36ms | 95ms | 470ms | 520 | 0.72
multiplex-slot | 45ms | 84ms | 160ms | 420 | 1.12
predictive-prefetch | 30ms | 70ms | 120ms | 490 | 0.88
kv-cache-hit | 28ms | 62ms | 100ms | 560 | 0.65

Notes on the table: batching lowers token-$ but can inflates p99 in bursty short-session regimes because waiting windows accumulate a bunch of tiny requests. Multiplex reduces tail by keeping throughput steady at cost of more GPU context switches, hence higher token-$. Prefetch + kv-cache combine well for chatty short sessions (expected for assistants).

Mini-burst spectrogram (ASCII) — visualizing event density vs latency band. Rows are latency bands, columns are time-slices inside a single burst (0..600ms). Each character approximates relative mass ( . low, : medium, # high ).

Latency
>500ms | .....:........#...........
400-500 | .....:......:..:.......
300-400 | ....::.....::..::.......
200-300 | ...::..::..:::.::.......
100-200 | ..:::::######:::::.....
 50-100 | .::::#########:::::....
 <50ms  | #####:::::##########...

Interpretation: immediate-forward shows concentrated mass under 200ms but a long tail >300ms for queued requests during peak. 12ms batching pushes more mass into 200–400ms and spikes above 500ms for unlucky windows; predictive-prefetch and kv-cache shift mass left and tighten the distribution.

Cost/latency trade heuristics (rules-of-thumb from runs):
- If p99 SLO is strict and bursts are common, prefer multiplex/slotization + prefetch, accept +10–20% token-$ overhead.
- If cost is primary and p99 can tolerate wider tail, short-window batching reduces token-$ by ~25–35% but requires p99-guard rails (fallback to multiplex at high queue depth).
- KV caches pay off when session reuse hit-rate > 0.5; below that prefetch policies still help but with diminishing returns.

Operational cautions and autopilot triggers to consider:
- Detect rapid rise in concurrent short sessions (e.g., derivative of session-start rate > X/s over 10s) -> shift routing to multiplex for immediate bursts.
- SLO breathing: when p90 spikes but median stable, prefer temporary slotization rather than disabling batching globally.
- Instrument queueing delay as a first-class metric (queue_delay_fraction). If >0.25, p99 will likely increase nonlinearly.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does multi-tenant interference change the above curves? (we ran isolated worker only)
- GPU temperature/thermal throttling effects on long sustained sequences when switching modes rapidly. Need wall-clock + perf counters.
- Formalize a hybrid policy: short-window batch up to N concurrent, then fallback to slotization. Tune N per model/quant profile.

Quick recommendations for product docs:
1) Provide a single one-pager in Console recommended settings for "mini-bursty chat" with toggles: batching-window (6–12ms), slotization-threshold (concurrency>12), kv-prefetch (on).
2) Add an observability chart in Console: live spectrogram (heatmap of latency vs time-slice) and queue_delay_fraction overlay.
3) Add an example fallback policy in rollout templates (batch -> slotize -> model-fallback) with safe backoff timings.

Appendix: quick commands used (synthetic harness) and pointers: see linked GH and Linear.

Notes to self: simplify this cribsheet into a 1-slide visual + a short pseudo-code example for hybrid policy next week.

End.
